about.title: San Marino Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: San Marino is a quiet, largely residential city, but workplace injuries still happen here — in offices along Huntington Drive, on landscaping and maintenance crews serving the city's estates, in retail spots near San Marino Avenue, and among contractors working on local properties. Under California law, workers' comp is usually the only path against your own employer, no matter who was at fault. But if a subcontractor, equipment manufacturer, or another company's employee contributed to your injury, you may have a separate claim worth exploring. San Marino's smaller commercial footprint means many injured workers aren't sure who to even report to, or whether a third party was involved. LawProactive doesn't practice law — we simply connect you with an independent attorney, free of charge, who can look at your paperwork, your timeline, and your options and explain what's realistic before deadlines pass.

whyChoose.title: Why San Marino Workers Turn to LawProactive

items.title: Clarity on Who You Can Actually Claim Against
items.desc: Workers' comp is usually your only path against your employer, but a negligent third party — like a subcontractor or equipment maker — can open a separate claim. An independent attorney can help you figure out which applies to your case.

items.title: Deadlines Don't Wait for Confusion
items.desc: You generally have 30 days to report a workplace injury to your employer, and third-party injury claims carry a 2-year deadline in California. Getting matched with an attorney early helps make sure nothing slips past those windows.

items.title: Protection From Retaliation
items.desc: California law makes it illegal for an employer to retaliate against you for reporting a workplace injury. An attorney in our network can explain your rights if you're worried about how reporting might affect your job.

items.question: I was hurt doing yard work on a private estate in San Marino — does workers' comp even apply?
items.answer: It depends on your employment relationship and who directed the work. If you were a W-2 employee of a landscaping company, workers' comp likely applies regardless of fault. If a property owner or another contractor's negligence contributed to your injury, there may also be a separate third-party claim worth reviewing.

items.question: What if my employer says I can't file a claim because I didn't report the injury right away?
items.answer: California generally gives you 30 days to report a workplace injury to your employer, so reporting late doesn't automatically end your claim. An independent attorney can look at the specific timeline and help you understand your options.

items.question: Can I be fired for reporting a workplace injury in San Marino?
items.answer: No — California law prohibits retaliation against employees who report workplace injuries. If you believe you were punished or let go for reporting, an attorney can review what happened and explain what protections may apply.
